prompt: What is a crossed molecular beam experiment?

choices.text: Two beams of atoms or molecules collided to study reaction dynamics
One beam of molecules fired at a solid target to study adsorption
choices.why: The experiment uses two gas-phase beams that meet each other, so the reaction studied is a collision between the two reactants.

choices.text: A laser beam crossed with a gas cell to measure its absorption
choices.why: Lasers were added later to excite the beams, but the experiment itself crosses two beams of atoms or molecules.

choices.text: Two gases mixed in a flask and sampled to follow concentrations
choices.why: Following concentrations in a mixture gives rates in bulk. Crossed beams look at the dynamics of individual reactive collisions.

explanation: In a crossed molecular beam experiment two beams of atoms or molecules are collided together to study the dynamics of a chemical reaction. It looks at single collisions rather than a bulk reacting mixture.

prompt: According to the section, what can crossed molecular beam experiments determine about the reaction products?

choices.text: Their velocity distribution and scattering angle
Only the overall rate constant at one temperature
choices.why: A bulk rate constant averages over all collisions. Crossed beams resolve individual collisions, giving product velocities and scattering angles.

choices.text: Their equilibrium concentrations
choices.why: Equilibrium is a property of a bulk mixture. Crossed beams follow products straight out of single collisions: their velocities and angles.

choices.text: Only their identity, not their motion
choices.why: Identity comes from the mass spectrometer, but the method's point is the motion: the distribution of velocities and the scattering angle.

explanation: The section says these experiments can detect individual reactive collisions and determine the distribution of velocities and the scattering angle of the products. Those are details a bulk rate measurement averages away.

prompt: Which statement about crossed molecular beam experiments does the section make?

choices.text: They can detect individual reactive collisions
They work only for reactions in solution
choices.why: Both beams are gas-phase atoms or molecules meeting in a vacuum chamber; the method is for gas-phase reactions.

choices.text: They measure only averages over many collisions
choices.why: The section stresses the opposite: they can detect individual reactive collisions, which bulk experiments can't.

choices.text: They need the beams to be as dense as possible
choices.why: Each beam is kept dilute enough to ignore collisions within it, so the only collisions are between the two beams.

explanation: Crossed molecular beam experiments can detect individual reactive collisions as well as the velocity and angular distributions of the products. That is what makes them a tool for reaction dynamics.

prompt: Why is each beam in a crossed molecular beam apparatus made dilute?

choices.text: So collisions within each beam can be ignored
So the beams travel faster
choices.why: Dilution isn't about speed. It ensures the molecules in a beam don't collide with each other, so only beam–beam collisions matter.

choices.text: So the products can't react again with the walls
choices.why: The walls aren't the issue the section raises. Each beam is dilute enough that collisions within it can be ignored.

choices.text: So the detector isn't saturated by product
choices.why: The section gives a different reason: dilute beams mean collisions within each beam can be ignored.

explanation: Each collimated beam is dilute enough to ignore collisions within it. The collisions that are observed are then the ones between a molecule of one beam and a molecule of the other.

prompt: In the section's description of the technique, what kind of beams intersect, and where?

choices.text: Two collimated gas beams, in a vacuum chamber
Two spreading gas jets, in air
choices.why: The beams are collimated, kept narrow and directed, and they meet in a vacuum chamber, not in air.

choices.text: Two liquid jets, in a vacuum chamber
choices.why: The beams are of gas-phase atoms or molecules. Only the vacuum chamber is right.

choices.text: Two collimated gas beams, in a buffer gas
choices.why: A buffer gas would add collisions the experiment is designed to avoid. The beams meet in a vacuum chamber.

explanation: The apparatus crosses two collimated beams of gas-phase atoms or molecules in a vacuum chamber. The direction and velocity of the product molecules leaving the crossing point are then measured.

prompt: In the apparatus of Figure 30.6.1a, what does each of the two molecular beams contain?

choices.text: Particles of a single reactant species
A mixture of both reactants
choices.why: If both reactants were in one beam they would collide before reaching the crossing point. Each beam carries one reactant species.

choices.text: One reactant and the products
choices.why: Products form only at the collision region where the beams meet. Each beam carries particles of a single reactant species.

choices.text: A reactant and a mass-spectrometer gas
choices.why: The mass spectrometer is the detector, not a beam ingredient. Each beam carries particles of a single reactant species.

explanation: The figure caption says each beam contains particles of a single reactant species. The two reactants meet only at the collision region, and the product particles travel away from there.

prompt: In Figure 30.6.1a, where are the product particles formed?

choices.text: At the collision region where the beams intersect
Inside each beam source
choices.why: Each source holds only one reactant species. Products form where the two beams meet, at the collision region.

choices.text: Inside the mass spectrometer
choices.why: The mass spectrometer detects products that have already formed. They form at the collision region and travel to it.

choices.text: On the walls of the vacuum chamber
choices.why: The reaction is between particles of the two beams, which meet in the collision region in the middle of the chamber.

explanation: The two beams intersect at the collision region, and the product particles travel away from it. A mass spectrometer then detects them.

prompt: In Figure 30.6.1a the product particles are detected by a mass spectrometer with a moveable inlet. What does moving the inlet allow?

choices.text: Catching products scattered in different directions
Changing the reactants' collision energy
choices.why: The collision energy is set by the beams, before the products reach the detector. Moving the inlet changes the direction it samples.

choices.text: Sending the products back into the beams
choices.why: The detector only samples products. Moving its inlet lets it receive products leaving at different scattering angles.

choices.text: Selecting which reactant enters the chamber
choices.why: Each beam source fixes its own reactant. The moveable inlet is on the detector, and it samples different directions.

explanation: The products travel away from the collision region in various directions, and the experiment measures their direction and velocity. A detector inlet that can be moved samples products at different angles, which gives the angular distribution.

prompt: The direction and velocity data are often coupled with mass spectrometric data. What does the combination reveal?

choices.text: How energy is partitioned among translation, rotation and vibration of the products
How energy is partitioned between the two reactant beams before they meet
choices.why: The beams' energies are set by the sources. The combined data concern the products: how their energy splits among translational, rotational and vibrational modes.

choices.text: Only the activation energy, from rates measured at several temperatures
choices.why: That is a bulk-kinetics measurement. Beam data instead show how the products' energy is shared among their modes of motion.

choices.text: Only the masses of the products, with no information about energy
choices.why: Masses come from the mass spectrometer alone. Together with direction and velocity, the data reveal the products' energy partitioning.

explanation: The section says direction and velocity measurements, coupled with mass spectrometry, yield the partitioning of energy among translational, rotational and vibrational modes of the product molecules.

prompt: Who developed the crossed molecular beam technique and shared the 1986 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it?

choices.text: Dudley Herschbach and Yuan T. Lee
Taylor and Datz
choices.why: Taylor and Datz, of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, first demonstrated the technique in 1953. Herschbach and Lee refined it and received the Nobel Prize.

choices.text: Dudley Herschbach and Taylor
choices.why: Taylor was half of the Oak Ridge pair who first demonstrated the technique. The prize went to Herschbach and Yuan T. Lee.

choices.text: Yuan T. Lee and Datz
choices.why: Datz worked with Taylor on the 1953 demonstration. The prize went to Yuan T. Lee and Dudley Herschbach.

explanation: Dudley Herschbach and Yuan T. Lee developed the crossed molecular beam technique and were awarded the 1986 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Taylor and Datz had demonstrated it earlier, in 1953.

prompt: According to the section, who first demonstrated the crossed molecular beam technique, and when?

choices.text: Taylor and Datz at Oak Ridge, in 1953
Herschbach and Lee, in 1953
choices.why: Herschbach and Lee came after the first demonstration; they refined the apparatus. The 1953 demonstration was by Taylor and Datz.

choices.text: Taylor and Datz at Oak Ridge, in 1986
choices.why: 1986 is the year of Herschbach and Lee's Nobel Prize. Taylor and Datz demonstrated the technique in 1953.

choices.text: Herschbach and Lee, in 1986
choices.why: 1986 is when Herschbach and Lee received the Nobel Prize for developing the technique, not when it was first demonstrated.

explanation: The technique was demonstrated in 1953 by Taylor and Datz of Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Herschbach and Lee later refined the apparatus, and won the 1986 Nobel Prize.

prompt: Since Taylor and Datz had already demonstrated crossed beams, what does the section credit Herschbach and Lee with?

choices.text: Refining the apparatus to probe reactions in unprecedented detail
Being the first to collide two molecular beams
choices.why: The first demonstration was Taylor and Datz's, in 1953. Herschbach and Lee refined the apparatus and probed gas-phase reactions in detail.

choices.text: Discovering that alkali metals ionize on a hot filament
choices.why: The section describes filament detection as an early method, not as Herschbach and Lee's discovery. Their contribution was refining the apparatus.

choices.text: Measuring the first rate constant of a gas reaction
choices.why: Rate constants were measured long before by bulk methods. Herschbach and Lee refined the beam apparatus to study reactions in detail.

explanation: Herschbach and Lee refined the crossed beam apparatus and began probing gas-phase reactions in unprecedented detail, work recognized by the 1986 Nobel Prize. The original demonstration was by Taylor and Datz.

prompt: Which elements did early crossed beam experiments investigate?

choices.text: Alkali metals such as K, Rb and Cs
Noble gases such as Ne, Ar and Kr
choices.why: The early experiments used alkali metals, because their detection method, ionization on a hot filament, works only for them.

choices.text: Main group elements such as C, N and O
choices.why: Main group elements needed new detection techniques, developed later. The early experiments studied alkali metals.

choices.text: Halogens such as F, Cl and Br
choices.why: The section names potassium, rubidium and cesium: alkali metals, which a hot filament detects efficiently.

explanation: Early crossed beam experiments investigated alkali metals such as potassium, rubidium and cesium. They could be detected by ionization on a hot metal filament.

prompt: How were scattered alkali metal atoms detected in early crossed beam experiments?

choices.text: They ionized on a hot metal filament, giving a small current
They emitted light when they struck a cold screen
choices.why: The section describes an electrical method, not an optical one: atoms hitting a hot filament ionized and produced a small current.

choices.text: They were sorted by a quadrupole mass filter
choices.why: Quadrupole mass filters were a later improvement. Early detection used a hot metal filament that ionized the alkali atoms.

choices.text: They were timed in a time-of-flight spectrometer
choices.why: Time-of-flight mass spectrometers came later, to measure kinetic energy. Early detectors were hot metal filaments.

explanation: When scattered alkali metal atoms hit a hot metal filament, they ionized and created a small electric current. Measuring that current detected the atoms.

prompt: Why was hot-filament detection of alkali atoms quite sensitive?

choices.text: The detection was nearly perfectly efficient
It measured each atom's kinetic energy
choices.why: The filament had no sensitivity to kinetic energy at all. Its sensitivity came from detecting nearly every atom that hit it.

choices.text: It could detect any element
choices.why: It was the opposite: it only detected alkali metals. For those it was nearly perfectly efficient, which made it sensitive.

choices.text: The beams were very dense
choices.why: The beams are dilute. The method was sensitive because nearly every alkali atom hitting the filament was ionized and counted.

explanation: Because nearly every alkali atom hitting the hot filament ionized and was counted, the detection was nearly perfectly efficient, and the technique was quite sensitive.

prompt: What was the main drawback of hot-filament detection that called for new techniques?

choices.text: It only detects alkali metals
It is too inefficient
choices.why: It was nearly perfectly efficient for what it could detect. The problem was that it could detect only alkali metals.

choices.text: It gives no angular information
choices.why: It actually gave a good indication of angular distribution. The problem was that it detects only alkali metals, not main group elements.

choices.text: It destroys the alkali atoms
choices.why: Ionizing the atoms is how the method works, not its drawback. The drawback was that only alkali metals could be detected.

explanation: The simple filament detector only detects alkali metals. New detection techniques were needed to analyze main group elements.

prompt: What did detection with a metal filament reveal about the scattered particles, and what did it miss?

choices.text: Angular distribution, but not kinetic energy
Kinetic energy, but not angular distribution
choices.why: It is the other way round. The filament gave a good indication of angular distribution but had no sensitivity to kinetic energy.

choices.text: Both angular distribution and kinetic energy
choices.why: The filament had no sensitivity to kinetic energy, which is why slotted disks were added to select velocities.

choices.text: Neither, only the total number of products
choices.why: Counting at different positions did give a good indication of angular distribution. It was kinetic energy that it missed.

explanation: Detection through a metal filament gave a good indication of angular distribution but had no sensitivity to kinetic energy. Velocity selectors were added to fill that gap.

prompt: Early apparatuses placed a pair of rotating slotted disks between the collision center and the detector. What did they do?

choices.text: Let through only particles with a certain known velocity
Let through only particles of a certain known mass
choices.why: Selecting by mass was the job of later quadrupole mass filters. The slotted disks selected by velocity.

choices.text: Chopped the reactant beams into short pulses
choices.why: The disks sat between the collision center and the detector, acting on the scattered particles. They passed only one velocity.

choices.text: Ionized the particles so they could be counted
choices.why: Ionization happened at the hot filament detector. The disks only passed particles with a certain known velocity.

explanation: By controlling the rotation speed of the slotted disks, only particles with a certain known velocity could pass through and be detected. This gave the kinetic energy information the filament alone couldn't.

prompt: With a pair of slotted disks as a velocity selector, what does the experimenter change to choose which particle velocity is detected?

choices.text: The rotation speed of the disks
The temperature of the filament
choices.why: The filament temperature affects ionization, not which velocities reach it. The velocity passed is set by how fast the disks rotate.

choices.text: The mass of the reactant atoms
choices.why: The velocity selector works on whatever particles arrive. Changing the disks' rotation speed changes which velocity gets through.

choices.text: The angle between the two beams
choices.why: That changes the collision, not the selection. The disks' rotation speed sets the velocity that can pass.

explanation: The section says that by controlling the rotation speed of the disks, only particles with a certain known velocity could pass through. Changing the speed selects a different velocity.

prompt: According to the section, which three kinds of information about the scattered species together give useful information about the dynamics of the system?

choices.text: Velocity, angular distribution and identity
Rate constant, activation energy and order
choices.why: Those come from bulk kinetics. A beam experiment gives the velocity, angular distribution and identity of the scattered species.

choices.text: Temperature, pressure and volume
choices.why: Those describe a bulk gas, not single collisions. The beam data are velocity, angular distribution and identity of the scattered species.

choices.text: Velocity, temperature and concentration
choices.why: Only velocity is right. The other two pieces are the angular distribution and the identity of the scattered species.

explanation: The section says that with information about the velocity, angular distribution and identity of the scattered species, useful information about the dynamics of the system can be derived.

prompt: What did adding quadrupole mass filters to crossed beam apparatuses allow?

choices.text: Selecting only the products of interest
Selecting only one product velocity
choices.why: Velocity selection was the job of slotted disks. Quadrupole mass filters select the products of interest.

choices.text: Exciting the beams before impact
choices.why: Exciting the beams is what lasers were added for. Quadrupole mass filters select the products of interest.

choices.text: Collimating the reactant gases
choices.why: Collimating the gases is what supersonic nozzles do. Quadrupole mass filters select only the products of interest.

explanation: Quadrupole mass filters let the detector select only the products of interest. Along with time-of-flight mass spectrometers, they allowed a vast array of compounds to be detected.

prompt: What did time-of-flight mass spectrometers add to crossed molecular beam experiments?

choices.text: Easy measurement of kinetic energy
Ionization of alkali atoms on a filament
choices.why: That was the early detection method. Time-of-flight mass spectrometers allowed easy measurement of kinetic energy.

choices.text: Collimation of the reactant beams
choices.why: Supersonic nozzles collimate the gases. Time-of-flight mass spectrometers made kinetic energy easy to measure.

choices.text: Selection of the beam's reactant species
choices.why: Each beam's species is set by its source. Time-of-flight instruments measure the products' kinetic energy.

explanation: Time-of-flight mass spectrometers allowed easy measurement of kinetic energy. With quadrupole mass filters, they let the apparatus detect a vast array of compounds.

prompt: What made the later crossed molecular beam apparatus "universal"?

choices.text: Mass-spectrometric detection of a vast array of compounds
Hot-filament detection of all the alkali metals
choices.why: Filament detection is limited to alkali metals, the opposite of universal. Mass filters and time-of-flight detection opened up a vast array of compounds.

choices.text: Velocity selection with rotating slotted disks
choices.why: Slotted disks added velocity information to early apparatuses. 'Universal' refers to detecting a vast array of compounds with mass spectrometry.

choices.text: Lasers that can excite any reactant beam
choices.why: Lasers broadened the technique further, but 'universal' refers to detection: mass spectrometry could handle a vast array of compounds.

explanation: Quadrupole mass filters and time-of-flight mass spectrometers allowed the detection of a vast array of compounds. This marked the advent of the 'universal' crossed molecular beam apparatus.

prompt: What were supersonic nozzles (Figure 30.6.1b) used for in crossed molecular beam experiments?

choices.text: To collimate the gases
To detect the products
choices.why: Detection is done by the mass spectrometer. Supersonic nozzles are on the source side, collimating the gases into beams.

choices.text: To select one product velocity
choices.why: Velocity selection was the job of slotted disks. Supersonic nozzles collimate the gases.

choices.text: To excite the molecules' vibrations
choices.why: Excitation was done with lasers. Supersonic nozzles collimate the gases, which expanded the scope of experiments.

explanation: Supersonic nozzles were used to collimate the gases, which expanded the variety and scope of experiments. Figure 30.6.1b shows such a supersonic molecular beam source.

prompt: How have lasers broadened the applicability of crossed molecular beam experiments?

choices.text: By exciting the beams, before impact or at the point of reaction
By heating the filament detector to ionize the atoms
choices.why: The filament is heated electrically and is an early detection method. Lasers are used to excite the beams.

choices.text: By replacing one of the two beams of molecules
choices.why: Both beams are still atoms or molecules. Lasers are used to excite them, either before impact or at the point of reaction.

choices.text: By collimating the gases into narrow beams
choices.why: Collimation is done by supersonic nozzles. Lasers excite the beams, before impact or at the point of reaction.

explanation: The use of lasers to excite the beams, either before impact or at the point of reaction, further broadened the applicability of the technique.

prompt: Which order of detection methods matches the history the section describes?

choices.text: Hot filament → slotted-disk velocity selector → quadrupole and time-of-flight mass spectrometry
Quadrupole and time-of-flight mass spectrometry → slotted-disk velocity selector → hot filament
choices.why: This is reversed. Hot-filament detection of alkali atoms came first, and mass spectrometry made the later 'universal' apparatus.

choices.text: Slotted-disk velocity selector → hot filament → quadrupole and time-of-flight mass spectrometry
choices.why: The slotted disks were added because the filament had no sensitivity to kinetic energy, so the filament came first.

choices.text: Hot filament → quadrupole and time-of-flight mass spectrometry → slotted-disk velocity selector
choices.why: Slotted disks were an early fix for the filament's lack of energy information; time-of-flight instruments later made kinetic energy easy to measure.

explanation: Early experiments detected alkali atoms on a hot filament, then added slotted disks to select velocities. Later, quadrupole mass filters and time-of-flight mass spectrometers gave the 'universal' apparatus.
